utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer; Sarah Clanton; Starroula Papadopoulos; case manager, Thomas Laugel; and legal intern, Ana Humljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, for the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning again, also to counsel. In our submissions today, I will be addressing legal issues first that arise out of the Defence submissions made on Monday. I will then address aspects of the joint criminal enterprise and how it relates to the Defence submissions from Monday. I'll also be addressing two of the four specific incidents that counsel identified as part of their challenge, those being Ovcara and the Velepromet. After I've completed my submissions, Mr. President, then my colleague, Sarah Clanton, will take the floor. She will address the other two incidents related to Opatovac and Lovas. She is also going to address other incidents, other aspects of the case, in which in our view the Court could find that there is sufficient evidence on all counts that the Defence has challenged. And she will also just -- she will also briefly address a couple of the other issues raised as part of the Defence submissions. Mr. President, Your Honours, at the hearing on Monday, the Defence clearly limited its 98 bis challenge to Counts 2 through 9 to the extent that they're based on four specific incidents or events and not counts, specifically the incidents at Velepromet, Ovcara, Lovas, Opatovac. The Defence also challenged Counts 5 through 9, but only to the extent that they are based on crimes committed in the camps that were located in Serbia. That's transcript 8988 and -89 from Monday's proceedings. Your Honours, the Chamber should reject the Defence invitation to engage in the piecemeal and incident-based application of Rule 98 bis that focuses only on parts of Counts 2 through 9 based on these four incidents. The Chamber should also decline to enter a judgement of acquittal regarding only those parts of Counts 5 through 9 that relate to the detention facilities in Serbia. The Defence's proposed application of Rule 98 bis is not only contrary to the plain language and intended of the Rule itself, it is also contrary to the consistent manner in which Trial Chambers have interpreted and applied Rule 98 bis since it was amended in 2004. As amended in 2004, the rule provides that the Chamber shall enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. The specific use of the word "count" is significant, it's not accidental. The word "count" was introduced in 2004 to replace the word "charge" which had appeared in the previous formulation of the Rule. On Monday, after citing Rule 98 bis as reformulated to focus on counts, my learned friend proceeded by referring to charges nonetheless, and it is indeed only a few specific charges that form the basis of the Rule 98 bis application. What was clear from my learned friend's presentation is that the Defence is not pleased with or does not suit them to apply Rule 98 bis as it ought to be applied and how it exists in its current version. Counsel indicated or claimed that counts and charges ought to be equivalent or that they are equivalent for purposes of 98 bis. That's page 8986. In support of this view, counsel claimed that Judge Robinson, in the Milosevic case, also considered charges and counts as equivalent; that's 8984. However, this is misleading, because Judge Robinson's views in the Milosevic case, of course, were expressed prior to the amendment of Rule 98 bis. What my learned friend omitted to mention is that Judge Robinson's views on Rule 98 bis after its amendment, for example, in Lukic and Lukic. We have a slide up for Your Honours and for counsel. This is page 3582 of the Lukic and Lukic case, where Judge Robinson states: "The rule, as amended in December 2004, focuses on counts rather than charges. If a count is comprised of several parts and there is no evidence on one part of the count but there is evidence capable of supporting a conviction on the other parts, the motion will fail." This was a unanimous decision, no dissent or separate opinion. This same approach and application is found in numerous other Rule 98 bis decisions entered by Chambers after the 2004 Rule change. Just for the Chamber's benefit, we're citing Mrksic decision from 28th June, 2006; Martic, 3 July 2006; Milutinovic, 18 May 2007; Prlic, 20 February 2008; Popovic, 3 March 2008; Lukic and Lukic, 13 November 2008; Gotovina, 3 April 2009; Seselj, 4th of May, 2011; Karadzic, 11 June 2012. These are all cases which have applied Rule 98 bis in the way it ought to be applied, by a counts approach, rather than entertaining specific incidents and purporting to strike or enter a judgement of acquittal as to a specific incident forming a part of a count. The Defence referred to Judge Antonetti's dissent in the Seselj case. What they did not mention is Judge Antonetti's statement in the Prlic case, which we've just cited here, which was unanimous. There

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI SAID
utterances.text: "Since the 8th of December, 2004, when Rule 98 bis was last amended, a Trial Chamber is only expected to determine whether the Prosecution has adduced enough evidence for each count taken as a whole, as opposed to all the various charges making up that particular count. As a consequence, the Trial Chamber may only enter a judgement of acquittal with respect to an entire count of the indictment." Now, when they referred to the Lukic and Lukic indictment, as well as the Haradinaj indictment on Monday, counsel essentially argued that 98 bis should apply to counts only when the count is based upon a single charge or a single incident, as was the case in those indictments. This approach would, in our view, Mr. President and Your Honours, effectively render 2004's amendment of 98 bis to be meaningless. The distinction between charges and counts with regard to the rule was noted by the Chamber in Karadzic, after it advised the parties that the Rule 98 bis submissions should be concerned with counts and not specific charges. And that's on the slide for Your Honours at this point. That's the Karadzic decision on accused's motion for order to withdraw unproven allegation, 23 May 2012, paragraph 3. I should say that it's in this decision, Mr. President, the Chamber did suggest that the Prosecution should go back and look at specific incidents. Of course there are many, many incidents in the Karadzic case, and invited the Prosecution to go back and to see whether there are any specific incidents which, in fairness or for whatever reason, ought to be dropped out of the case at that stage. And the Prosecution agreed to undertake that. In this case, it's our submission that there are no incidents in which there has been a failure of proof, none. So that again the counts-based approach is what's required under the law, and proceeding on that basis certainly isn't going to result in any inefficiency because of the possibility that an individual incident here or there might have actually been left unproved. In advocating a return to the charge or incident-based approach to Rule 98 bis, the Defence has also referred to the structure of the Hadzic indictment. However, our indictment is entirely consistent with the approach taken in other leadership cases. The indictments in Martic, Karadzic, Seselj, all have counts also which are comprised of different, separate incidents. During the Rule 98 bis proceedings in those cases, the Chambers determined whether for each count there was sufficient evidence capable of supporting a conviction for at least one of the criminal incidents and the accused's responsibility for it. We say that's the correct approach and the approach taken by the Defence here asking the Court to focus on specific incidents as opposed to the counts as a whole is not a correct application of the Rule. My learned friend also indicated that it's more efficient, perhaps more fair, to consider specific locations or incidents. In our view, Mr. President, the amendment to Rule 98 bis was intended to make the proceedings more efficient by eliminating the requirement that each charge has to be considered individually. The fact that a count is made up of several incidents was acknowledged by Judge Robinson himself. In the Dragomir Milosevic Rule 98 bis decision, this is what he said, this is from Dragomir Milosevic, 3 May 2007, transcript in that case, 5641 and -42: "Thus, a count could have as many as 100 or more separate allegations. It could cover 40 municipalities, be alleged completed by 15 different mean, details of which could be set out in 50 or more items ..." He goes on: "As presently formulated and applied, a submission leading to the acquittal of the accused or of an accused at the end of the Prosecution case is only likely to succeed in the very rare case when the Prosecution case, as a whole, has broken down, so that there is no evidence of either the actus reus or the mens rea of the crime." And, Mr. President, we say that there is no aspect of the case in which there has been a failure of proof remotely close to that level of collapse. It's our submission, Mr. President, Your Honours, that the Chamber can deny the Defence Rule 98 bis application on this ground. The Defence has not even attempted to demonstrate that there was a failure of proof on any count in the indictment. They have only focused on four specific incidents out of the many that are found in the case. The Defence also argued that this is a circumstantial case and that, therefore, inferential findings, inferences, can only be entered at the Rule 98 bis stage when they are the only reasonable inference or conclusion that can be drawn, that's at transcript 8975, 8991. That is factually and legally incorrect. Factually, we do not accept that this is a circumstantial case. This is a case with abundant direct evidence of Goran Hadzic's criminal intent, direct evidence of his significant contribution to the joint criminal enterprise, direct evidence of his participation in the events, and indeed in some of the crimes themselves that occurred. There's nothing circumstantial about that. Legally it is also incorrect to say that this is a circumstantial case or that, as a result, the Chamber has to draw all inferences or has to rule out all inferences apart from guilt basically in order to proceed. There is clear case law on this. At the Rule 98 bis stage, inferences do not have to be the only inferences reasonably available on the evidence. The Chamber in Popovic squarely addressed the issue and stated that: "At the ... 98 bis stage, the inference of an agreement to commit genocide need not be the only reasonable inference that could be drawn from the evidence." This is Popovic, 3rd of March, 2008, their transcript number 21464. Indeed, for the Chamber to accept the Defence application to apply this strict inferential standard at this stage would run contrary to the practice and the rule that the Chamber accepts the Prosecution evidence at its highest. Applying Rule 98 bis to the evidence at hand, to counts, and accepting the Prosecution evidence at its highest, we submit the Defence has failed to meet its high burden of showing that there is any count for which a judgement of acquittal should be entered. With regard to the detention facilities located in Serbia, the Defence raises a legal question whether international humanitarian law applies in Serbia. This argument begins on page 9023 of Monday's transcript. The Defence question whether there was an armed conflict or a spillover of an armed conflict into Serbia, and therefore whether IHL applies there, is the question that was raised by counsel on Monday. Our first response to that is that, as is the case with the other four substantive incidents which the Defence raised linking those to OG South, this assertion that with respect only to the detention facilities in Serbia this is yet again a piecemeal, incident-based argument that's inappropriate for consideration under the applicable Rule 98 bis standard. There is by no means a complete failure of proof on the detention-related crimes charged in Counts 5 to 9 and there is indeed no challenge raised to the detention crimes alleged to have occurred in places, for example, such as Erdut and Dalj. Again, it's a specific incident-based approach that's inappropriate under Rule 98 bis. Secondly, this is a novel legal question, raised for the first time in this case on Monday in the form of an oral submission. Counsel refers to no legal authority or precedent supporting his view that the prisoners in Serbia did not merit the protection of international humanitarian law simply because they had been transported into Serbia. And yet the Defence asked the Chamber to remove parts of Counts 5 to 9 regarding the charged detention facilities in Serbia and the crimes such as mistreatment and the sexual violence that occurred in those facilities on the basis of a legal argument raised for the first time on Monday. Although Chambers are not precluded from making determinations of legal issues at the 98 bis stage, the Tribunal case law after the 2004 amendment indicates that generally they refrain from doing so. The Trial Chamber should refrain from doing so here. Here are some examples of issues that were not considered appropriate for determination at the 98 bis phase. We have the slide up. These come from the Popovic case, 3 March 2008, transcript 21462-63, 21465-66, 68; Milutinovic decision 14 June 2007, paragraph 18; Kvocka, decision on motions for acquittal, 15 December 2000, paragraph 41. Legal issues raised which the Chambers declined to consider at the 98 bis stage, including such issues as whether victims of deportation as a crime against humanity must be civilians, whether the Prosecution had alleged two conspiracies based on the same conduct, definition of forcible transfer, et cetera. So in our view, Mr. President, that's another reason why the Chamber should not take up the issue of the Serbian detention facilities, which, as raised on Monday, is a purely legal question whether international law applies to the victims, the prisoners, who were held there. If the Chamber were minded to consider the merits of the Defence submission on the applicability of international humanitarian law, the Prosecution offers these brief submissions, although we believe that such a question is indeed best left until the end of the proceedings, if ever, and only then on written submissions in which both parties have been afforded sufficient time to research and develop their positions. In fairness, we should get more time to address this purely legal issue. Having said that, we offer these brief and possibly incomplete submissions, based upon what we've been able to develop as a response in the limited time that we've been given. Before arriving at the Serbian detention facilities, many of those prisoners who testified in this case first had to endure the siege and the destruction of Vukovar. When the town fell on the 18th of November, they emerged from their destroyed homes, cellars, shelters. They were rounded up by the JNA and they were transported to Serbia. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI SAID
utterances.text: Therefore, the rounding up and the detention of these prisoners undoubtedly occurred in the context of the armed conflict in Vukovar and the surrounding area. The crimes inflicted on these prisoners in the Serbian camps occurred in the context of the armed conflict and are clearly connected to the conflict, even though the detention crimes occurred in Serbia. How can it be that after being bombed out of their homes, rounded up, and transported to detention camps by the JNA, these victims lost the protection of international humanitarian law simply because they had been removed to Serbia? In the Seselj case, the Appeals Chamber held that for purposes of Article 5, crimes against humanity: "The Prosecution need only establish that an armed conflict is sufficiently related to the crimes with which the accused is charged." The Chamber has that on the screen, Seselj decision on the interlocutory appeal concerning jurisdiction, 31 August 2004, paragraphs 12 to 14. To this end: "It is sufficient to show a connection between the Article 5 crime itself and the armed conflict." For Article 3 crimes, the Prosecution must show a nexus to the armed conflict. In Stakic, the Appeals Chamber stated at paragraph 342: "For Article 3 to apply, the crime charged must be committed in a time of armed conflict and an accused's acts must be closely related to the conflict. The latter requirement is known as the 'nexus' requirement. The nexus need but not be a causal link, 'but the existence of an armed conflict must, at a minimum, have played a substantial part in the perpetrator's ability to commit the crime, his decision to commit it, the manner in which it was committed, or the purpose for which it was committed.'" And here the Chamber cites the Kunarac appeal judgement at paragraph 58. This is Stakic, 22 March 2006, paragraph 342. Your Honours, we submit that the nexus between the crimes at the Serbian crimes and the armed conflict is self-evident. The facts and circumstances of their detention and mistreatment demonstrate a clear link between the victims in the Serbian camps, the crimes committed against them there, and the armed conflict from which they came before finding themselves in the Serbian camps. In particular, even if the detainees were only entitled to the protections available in non-international armed conflicts, that is, Common Article 3, they would be protected from the inhumane treatment which they suffered. It would be nonsensical if these protections could be circumvented by simply moving detainees a certain distance or even across a border. The Geneva Conventions and Common Article 3, in particular, are part of customary international law, applicable to both international and non-international armed conflicts. Regardless of how one characterises the conflict or the fact that the victims had been transported from Vukovar to camps in Serbia, these people cannot be stripped of the protections to which they're entitled under Common Article 3. And that is because of the close, virtually seamless, nexus that exists between these prisoners, the crimes visited upon them in the Serbian camps, and the armed conflict from which they emerged in Vukovar. We consider the Defence's challenge to crimes occurring in Serbia at the detention facilities to be a wholly legal challenge, the one that I've just addressed. There is no claim that the crimes did not occur, nor is there a claim that Hadzic is not responsible for them under one of the alleged modes of liability. The claim is that IHL does not apply. Having addressed that point here, we do not intend to make further factual submissions related to the Serbia detention facilities. Finally some remarks on the legal side with regard to counsel's characterisation of aspects of the law of joint criminal enterprise. On Monday counsel repeatedly asserted that the accused must intend or know the details of a specific incident falling within a common criminal purpose in order to be held responsible. For example, in relation to the killings at Lovas minefield, counsel argued that a "precondition" for Hadzic's liability would be a pre-existing or contemporaneous knowledge of the incident. That's page 9014 of the transcript. This argument is based on a fundamental misunderstanding of the law of this Tribunal. The Defence supported their argument by referring to Brdjanin, the appeal judgement, paragraph 430. This paragraph concerns JCE liability and indeed JCE is a mode of liability that the Prosecution alleges in this case. However, Brdjanin does not stand for the proposition that the Defence claims. In Brdjanin the Appeals Chamber held that for JCE liability it must be shown that the JCE member shares the intent for the crimes within the JCE. By "crimes," this means crimes set out in the Statute of the Tribunal, such as murder as a war crime or crime against humanity, forcible transfer, torture, et cetera. This does not mean that the accused has to intend or be aware of all the details of the specific criminal incidents occurring on the ground. The Appeals Chamber has confirmed this in numerous cases; for example, in Krajisnik the Appeals Chamber held at paragraph 200: "The Appeals Chamber notes that the Trial Chamber correctly identified the required mens rea for the first form of JCE, explaining that it must be shown that 'the JCE participants, including the accused, had a common state of mind, namely the state of mind that the statutory crimes forming part of the objective should be carried out ...'" Here the Appeals Chamber referred to the statutory crimes. It did not require the Chamber to look at the accused's specific state of mind and conduct in relation to every underlying incident. Mr. President, I believe that a redaction may be needed at page 11, line 4, I've just been passed a note. I may have mentioned a name that I shouldn't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll check that, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Appeals Chamber jurisprudence establishes -- excuse me, I need to back up. The Defence also erroneously claims that the accused must specifically or directly contribute to each underlying incident, again such as the murders at Lovas minefield. See, for example, transcript 9014. Here counsel stated, "Now, even assuming..." These are the words of counsel, my learned friend, on Monday: "Even assuming that there is some potential association between Mr. Hadzic and Mr. Bogic, there is no indication that Mr. Bogic shared any information about the incident, much less that Bogic was the conduit for conveying any instructions that would have contributed to this crime." We say that's not necessary or required as a contribution under JCE. The Appeals Chamber jurisprudence establishes that the accused's significant contribution should go to the common criminal purpose. As the Appeals Chamber in Kvocka held, paragraph 263: "Contrary to Kvocka's claim, to find an accused guilty of the crime of murder it is not necessary to establish his participation in each murder. For crimes committed as part of a joint criminal enterprise, it is sufficient to prove not the participation of the accused in the commission of the specific crime but the responsibility of the accused in furthering the common criminal purpose. The Appeals Chamber finds that the Trial Chamber did not err in finding Kvocka guilty of the crime of murder without establishing his specific responsibility for each murder committed." By contributing to the common criminal purpose, the accused contributes to the crimes falling within the JCE. This is why the appeals jurisprudence does not require direct participation in each specific crime charged. Mr. President, that completes our legal submissions. With those arguments, it's our submission that applying correctly the law and the practice of Rule 98 bis, the Defence arguments concerning the state of jurisprudence on personal responsibility at this Tribunal correctly. This is a basis on which the Chamber can deny the motion or motions for judgement of acquittal, to the extent that they are directed at pieces of the case, specific incidents forming a relatively small number of the total number of incidents on which the counts are based. If the Chamber applies 98 bis correctly, there are no counts to dismiss because the Defence has not identified any count for which there has been a failure of proof. This alone is sufficient for the Chamber to deny now, at this time, the Defence motion without any further input or response from the Prosecution. The Chamber should not entertain the incident-based challenges advanced by the Defence. I'm not getting the signal that the Chamber's prepared to accept our suggestion on that point, and so I will continue with my submissions. The Prosecution is, Mr. President, prepared to proceed with additional submissions in order to show that even the relatively small number of incidents which the Defence now seeks to challenge falls squarely within the scope of the joint criminal enterprise charged in the indictment and are incidents for which Goran Hadzic bears individual criminal responsibility. In what remains of my submissions, I will refer the Chamber to evidence showing that Hadzic intended these crimes, these statutory crimes, and that he contributed to the JCE in which they were committed. I will address the Defence's challenge to the Ovcara and Velepromet incidents. My colleague, Ms. Clanton, then, as indicated, will refer the Chamber to more specific evidence related to the other two incidents, Opatovac and Lovas, and to other incidents charged in Counts 2 through 9 which make it clear that there is ample evidence to support each of those counts for purposes of this hearing. Goran Hadzic bears individual criminal responsibility for what we call the four incidents because he shared the intent that the crimes charged in Counts 2 through 9 would be committed against non-Serbs as part of the common purpose of the JCE. He knew and intended that murders, beatings, unlawful imprisonment, and torture would be committed in furtherance of the joint criminal enterprise, even if he was not personally present when every incident occurred. The physical perpetrators of crimes charged in the four incidents were members of this joint criminal enterprise with Hadzic or else were tools used by JCE members. Hadzic, as the most senior and powerful Serb political figure in the SBWS, significantly contributed to this enterprise. And so if we are to engage in an incident-based analysis of the evidence for purposes of this hearing, the Chamber would, in our respectful submission, benefit from a look-back at some of the evidence it has heard and seen that tells us about Hadzic's criminal intent and contribution to the JCE generally. Before this, however, I do have a couple of preliminary remarks. First, the Defence raises no challenge with respect to any counts or crimes that were committed in the SAO Krajina region and no challenge to crimes that occurred during 1992 and 1993. We will, therefore, not address those crimes. We will, however, refer to some pieces of evidence from that period that shed light on Hadzic's intent during 1991. Secondly, as mentioned already, the fact that Hadzic was not personally present when every crime was committed does not make this a circumstantial case. On a few occasions Monday my learned friend asserted just that, transcript 8975 and -76. As said, our case is a direct case, direct evidence of Hadzic's intent, direct evidence of his contribution to the common criminal purpose. As president of the SBWS, Goran Hadzic -- sorry, as president of the SBWS government, Goran Hadzic made clear his government's policy and his own personal view that there was no place for non-Serbs in the Serb-controlled territories in Croatia. Hadzic repeatedly and publicly advocated ethnic separation of Serbs and non-Serbs. His tactic of demonising Croats in his public statements made clear that they were a fair target for crimes such as those charged in Counts 2 through 9, whether in Erdut, Beli Manastir, Lovas, or Ilok. His views manifested themselves on the ground in the crimes that we have, in our view, proven in this case. For example, in a press conference in September of 1991, after claiming that Vukovar would be the capital of the SAO SBWS, Hadzic distinguished between "indigenous Croats" as opposed to Croats who arrived after World War II. He claimed that some of the Croat population carried a hatred of Serbs in their genes. The non-indigenous Croats who in previous generations had settled in these areas from western Herzegovina would be given return tickets. Hadzic further stated that "we" do not have problems with colonised Serbs who are extremists. That's P39 and P2955.2913. The Chamber will recall the evidence of Witness Veljko Dzakula, a prominent Serbian politician in Croatia. He reviewed this report that I've just described and confirmed that such statements provoked hatred, distrust and fear among Serbs and Croats alike, having come from a member of the Croatian Serb leadership. He confirmed that Hadzic advocated population movements: Serbs in, Croats out, prevention of Croat returns, transcript 394-395. By March of 1992, Hadzic, with the assistance of Serb forces such as Arkan's volunteer guard and the JNA units deployed throughout SBWS, had substantially achieved the goal of cleansing non-Serbs from the territory. As implementation of the Vance Plan approached, Hadzic advocated for population movements in the opposite direction. At the SFRY Presidency meeting in Belgrade on the 2nd of March, 1992, Hadzic and Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic had an exchange on the issue of population movements and exchanges. Karadzic observed that the idea of organised population exchange was nebulous and would be seen as abhorrent by the rest of the world. Hadzic disagreed saying: "There is nothing nebulous in it. The Serbs from Zagreb should resettle, as well as those from Belgrade, and it is out of the question now." That's P37, page 68; transcript 384-385. Hadzic and Arkan intimidated and threatened even Serbs who did not support their vision of an ethnically pure SBWS. The Chamber will recall the testimony again of Mr. Dzakula, who in late March or April of 1992 met with Hadzic in Hadzic's office in Erdut. Arkan was also present. Hadzic asked Veljko Dzakula: "Is it true that you advocate co-existence with the Croats?" Dzakula denied that he advocated co-existence because he was afraid of the consequences of admitting it in the presence of Arkan. As Dzakula said, Arkan was "quite ruthless to people who did not express Serbdom as he thought was fit." That's transcript 379-380, 413, 570-572. And indeed, the Chamber will recall subsequently that in the spring of 1993 Mr. Dzakula was stripped of his membership in the RSK Assembly and jailed for having signed the Daruvar Agreement, which was an agreement he made with Croatian authorities that was intended to create preconditions for the return of refugees to Western Slavonia. Goran Hadzic signed a decree disbanding the Western Slavonia regional council through which Hadzic had entered into the Daruvar Agreement, P44, P45, P46, transcript 403-405, 413-417. In a July 1992 meeting with UNPROFOR Commander Nambiar, Hadzic claimed he was willing to accept the return of non-Serbs, that it must be realised that "even if all non-Serbs were to return, the Serbs would still remain in the majority." That's P41, paragraph 10. Hadzic was clearly in favour of taking advantage of ethnic cleansing committed under his regime to maintain the Serb majority where there had not even been one prior to the conflict. On the 4th of September, 1992, when confronted by UN Under-Secretary-General Marek Goulding with the ethnic cleansing of non-Serbs that was continuing in Sector East in the SBWS region, Hadzic defended the practice saying that they should act "eye for eye and tooth for tooth" because of the expulsion of Serbs from areas of Western Slavonia, P2432.2398. In our submissions on the JCE, I will refer the Chamber to evidence of Hadzic's broad powers as SBWS prime minister and his relations with several of the various Serb forces that were on the ground in the SBWS contributing to the common criminal purpose. The Chamber should consider all of this evidence to come in light of the personal views expressed by Goran Hadzic throughout the period covered by this case, his views on ethnic separation, ethnic engineering, demographic engineering, if you will, and consider that evidence now in light of how he's acting with other JCE members, Serb forces, during 1991. We know from Theunens that the mission of the JNA changed. After first, of course, having been the army of all of Yugoslavia and then initially acting as a buffer between conflicting parties in Croatia, the JNA eventually became a Serb armed force for the Serb people in Croatia. This is clearly visible from early operations in July and August 1991 during the take-over of Dalj and Erdut. That's Theunens, transcript 4150-4153; P1753, pages 141-142; P2930. We also know that the JNA accepted for operational purposes Serbian volunteers linked to political parties and/or otherwise known for undisciplined and violent behaviour, such as the Leva Supoderica, party linked to the Serbian Radical Party of Mr. Seselj; the Dusan Silni, which was active in Lovas; and of course the Serbian Volunteer Guard, Arkan and his men. Exhibit 2937, transcript 4128, 4649; Exhibit 1753, pages 124-125; D17; and P1865. The JNA's having accepted volunteers for operational purposes is important because it shows the interrelation between the various Serb forces in the SBWS: The JNA, Arkan, volunteers, and the local TO, the SBWS Territorial Defence. The Defence attempt on Monday to try to describe OG South as some separate organisational structure bearing no link to Hadzic or other members of the JCE, does not reflect the evidence. I'm referring to counsel's remarks on Monday at page 8991. This issue of OG South/OG North is a red herring. Whether or not there is some sort of organisational structure connecting Hadzic to crimes in OG South is irrelevant. What matters is whether the crimes committed there are linked to Hadzic or one of his fellow JCE members. In his submissions on Monday, Defence sought to create this distinction between OG North and OG South, even suggesting that there might be two JCEs in this case: One in the north, one in the south. Transcript 9012. The 98 bis challenge that they raise relates to the four incidents which they say took place in OG South. Your Honours, there are not two JCEs in this case. There is a single JCE, a single joint criminal enterprise, for purposes of this hearing which encompass the entire territory of the SBWS, that is, the entire territory for which Goran Hadzic acted as prime minister during 1991. The JCE members operating on the territory of the SBWS included: Hadzic, as the prime minister; Arkan and his Serbian Volunteer Guard; the SBWS TO; Serb volunteers such as Leva Supoderica; Stevo Bogic and the Serbian National Security unit, which was based just metres away from Mr. Hadzic's office in Erdut; and of course the JNA. JNA forces in the SBWS were all under the command of the JNA 1st Military District and its commander, Zivota Panic, P2931, P2933, P2940, P1986.1981. Your Honours see a slide. This is from the expert report of Mr. Theunens, Exhibit P1753. This is at page 197. And in describing the respective areas of responsibility within the territory of the SBWS, he refers here to the north. "OG North is based on the 12th Novi Sad Corps, commanded by Major-General Andrija Biorcevic ..." Biorcevic's predecessor, I should add, was General Bratic. The Trial Chamber will recall the video footage of the dinner celebration in which Biorcevic described how his units, his JNA units, of OG North worked in close co-ordination with Hadzic. The video is P211.140. He celebrated Arkan and worked jointly with him in his operations in OG North. We say that Biorcevic, the JNA, and Arkan were all acting jointly in the north to further the common criminal purpose. The next slide relates to the Vukovar area. In the middle of the SBWS, corresponding to the eastern Slavonia/Vukovar area, Colonel Mrksic was in command. His area of responsibility was Vukovar, extending south to Ovcara and Grabovo. Here again we're relying on the Theunens report, 1753, pages 197 and 198. We say that the JNA's complete and utter destruction of Vukovar was intended to advance the common criminal purpose by installing Vukovar as the capital of the SBWS with Hadzic as its president, and in the process to drive out the non-Serb civilian population there. Vukovar was better defended and it took longer to conquer than the other places in the SBWS. However, the purpose of the attack on Vukovar, the intent to achieve Serb domination over the town, is qualitatively no different from the JNA attacks to the north or to the south in Western Srem. This also was a part of the common criminal plan. After the town fell, the JNA removed the inhabitants of Vukovar, in many cases transporting them to the JNA camps in Serbia where now it's claimed they no longer had any protection under international humanitarian law. In the south, again from the Theunens report page 198 of Exhibit P1753, the area of Western Srem, including Lovas, Tovarnik, Bapska, Sarengrad, Ilok, these comprised the area of responsibility of Major-General Arandjelovic. I'll speak in a few minutes about how the JNA in Western Srem conducted its activities in a way that was consistent with the JNA forces to the north. But first, in Monday's submissions the Defence claimed that Hadzic was not responsible for the Lovas and Opatovac incidents because they fall inside the JNA's Operative Group South. That's not correct. The Chamber has visited these places on the site visit. You will recall that all of these places are in Western Srem. And as we see here on the slide, Lovas is specifically in the area of responsibility of Arandjelovic, not the Operative Group South, which is under Mrksic's command farther to the north and which is restricted primarily to the Vukovar town. Opatovac is down here as well. The Chamber may recall Lovas, Tovarnik, Bapska. It's on the road between those various towns in Western Srem, all outside of the OG South, in the area of responsibility of Arandjelovic. Whatever might be the Defence theory as to why Hadzic is not responsible for crimes committed in OG South, that theory does not apply to Lovas and Opatovac. Regarding Western Srem, as Arkan and Biorcevic were working together in the northern third of the SBWS where Hadzic was based, doing their part to further the criminal common purpose by attacking and expelling non-Serbs there, Arandjelovic and his JNA forces were busily ridding the SBWS territory of the non-Serbs who lived in Western Srem, places whose name we see, Lovas, Tovarnik, Bapska, Sarengrad, Ilok, for example. Arandjelovic, his JNA forces in the south contributing to the same common purpose as the pounding, the destruction of Vukovar, which is intended to achieve the same result also being sought by Biorcevic, Arkan, and Hadzic's own backyard in the north, it's all the same, top to bottom, north to south. The OG South/OG North distinction bears no relevance to the Chamber's consideration of the evidence in this case or the joint criminal enterprise. On the 27th of September 1991, a Bora Tomic delivered an ultimatum to the inhabitants of Bapska. It was signed by JNA Major Slobodan Barjaktarevic, who was under the command of Major-General Arandjelovic. The Chamber has the ultimatum. I'm not going to bring it up or read it, but it made clear that if the people of Bapska did not surrender the village would be erased from the map. The ultimatum was read out on Croatian TV, P324, paragraphs 13 to 16; P316, page 1. Arandjelovic was involved in the expulsion of the non-Serbs inhabitants of Ilok. During the negotiations leading up to the expulsion - this is October 1991 - Arandjelovic threatened the Croat representatives from Ilok if they did not surrender their weapons: "I am going to use tanks and howitzers and aircraft and I'm going to level Ilok to the ground." That's the statement attributed to Arandjelovic by Witness Brletic, P1418, transcript 1338.
