utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Also just to -- I failed to mention the -- give a citation on the Kvocka, this -- on the legal submissions on contribution referred to the Kvocka appeals judgement decision or the appeals judgement, I should say, and just for the record that's the 25th of February, 2005, paragraph 263. I didn't give that citation on page 15, lines 14 to 15, today which would have been the place to do it. Shall I -- could I also indicate for the record, Mr. President, that we're now joined in the courtroom by our intern, Mr. Kat Tai Tam, who's joining us for the remainder of today's proceedings. One last loose end -- one last loose end, Mr. President. On the issue of the Vukovar, we would like to direct the Chamber to the testimony of Mr. Theunens at 4296-4297, also P1694. And this relates to a ceremony or recognition of the 1st Military District of the JNA which was given to the efforts of the volunteers for their contribution to the Vukovar operation and this was held at the SSNO, that's the secretariat for the people's defence in Belgrade, at a reception on the 21st of November, 1991. And to congratulate JNA officers involved in -- who were in charge of the operation at Vukovar, Mile Mrksic, Andrija Biorcevic, Zivota Panic, who was the commander of the 1st military district. Noting also that Vukovar TO member Miroljub Vujovic was also present with Kadijevic who was the secretary for All People's Defence at the reception in his office. And so we see that as a broader, more JNA-membership-based piece of evidence that relates to the Vukovar operation as well as Ovcara. With regard to Velepromet, Your Honours, the Prosecution position is that Hadzic bears responsibility for the crimes committed at Velepromet as charged in Counts 2 through 9 because the perpetrators of the crimes were linked to members of the JCE of which Hadzic was a member. This applies whether the perpetrators were JNA, local TO, or volunteers. The evidence shows that the perpetrators of the crimes committed at Velepromet were both members of the JNA, Vukovar TO, and volunteers. As counsel indicated in his submissions on Monday, the JNA acquiesced in the crimes committed against prisoners by others such as volunteers who were permitted to enter the Velepromet compound; that's transcript 9016. Even if TO members or Chetniks committing crimes were subordinated to the JNA at the time or had been subordinated to the JNA for operational purposes as counsel asserts at page 9016 of the transcript, this still does not sever or break the link between the crimes, the perpetrators and Hadzic in the JCE. Of course, as set out in our earlier submissions, the TO SBWS members were subordinates of Goran Hadzic. And I'm going to direct the Chamber to additional evidence on that issue shortly. This does not change even if they had been temporarily subordinated to the JNA. Those perpetrators at Velepromet were clearly carrying out crimes that form a part of the JCE, crimes that Hadzic intended and accepted. Furthermore, both the JNA and TO units were closely co-operating with members of the SBWS government and the other Serb forces, such as Chetnik volunteers used by the JCE members during the implementation of the JCE. For example, counsel claims that Velepromet was a JNA headquarters under the control of the JNA; that's Monday's transcript at 9016. However, as we know, the Velepromet facility was indeed used by Hadzic and his government as the site of the important government meeting held there on the 20th during which the fate of the Ovcara prisoners was decided. This is yet another example of the collaboration between the various JCE actors, Serb forces, and Hadzic's government. We note some ambiguity in the Defence position in respect of Velepromet, and I do wish also to highlight briefly errors in counsel's characterisation of what must be proved in relation to Hadzic's knowledge and intent regarding crimes at Velepromet. In his submissions counsel initially referred to challenging the Velepromet crimes that occurred on 19 November 1991; that's page 8988 of Monday's transcript. However, in the course of the submissions on Velepromet, the Defence referred to the evidence of GH-063. 63 was not present at Velepromet until the 21st of November, after he had been returned from Ovcara on the night of the 20th, spent the night at a place called Modateka and then brought to Velepromet on the 21st where he spent time with others in the room of death and the carpentry workshop, the Stolarija; that's transcript of GH-063, 8670 and -71. So there is somewhat of a disconnect in terms of the time-frame, 19, 20, 21, involving the crimes at Velepromet and precisely what the Defence is challenging. Counsel's also mis-characterised the law, in our view, again in terms of what is required to prove Hadzic's knowledge and involvement and responsibility for crimes at Velepromet. At page 9016 and 9017 of Monday's hearing, my learned friend says, I'm quoting: "There has to be evidence that he knows, starting with knowledge, there has to be knowledge that these crimes are taking place or will take place. He," referring to Hadzic, "has to have at least an awareness that that's going to occur; and if he doesn't, then there cannot be liability for those crimes." We would just simply refer the Chamber to our earlier submissions on the knowledge requirement in respect of Hadzic's liability for these crimes as a member of the joint criminal enterprise, particularly the Krajisnik Appeals Chamber judgement at paragraph 200 in which the Appeals Chamber stated the Trial Chamber had correctly identified the required mens rea for the first form of JCE, explaining that it must be shown that the JCE participants, including the accused, had a common state of mind; namely, the state of mind that the statutory crimes forming part of the JCE objective should be carried out. So we do not have to prove Hadzic's knowledge of the specific incidents, as was asserted by my learned friend on Monday, for every beating, every murder, every incident that occurred at Velepromet during the 19th, the 20th, or the 21st. In our submissions we will address the composition of the Serb forces that were at the Velepromet facility during the three-day period of 19 to 21 November, which is the period that corresponds to paragraph 31 of the indictment, as set out in annex 1. There is no dispute that Hadzic was present at Velepromet on the 20th. However, Mr. President, Your Honours, it's the Prosecution position that because the crimes committed at Velepromet were all linked to co-JCE members of Hadzic, his presence or not at Velepromet at the moment that any given crime was committed is not decisive in respect of his criminal liability. Your Honours have heard evidence that non-Serbs were detained at Velepromet from early November 1991 under the control of the JNA, Exhibit P2285.2284, which is a report drafted by the Guards Motorised Brigade security organ. Your Honours have also heard from victims and survivors that non-Serbs were detained at Velepromet following the fall of Vukovar on the 18th of November, 1991. They testified before the Chamber that the guards at Velepromet were members of the Vukovar TO. Referring here to P2506, transcript 4008-4013, 4035-36. That on the 19th of November there were paramilitaries wearing all sorts of clothing. Also Covic, P067.1, transcript 3441.3443, referring to a member of the Territorial Defence and members of the Territorial Defence at Velepromet being in charge. GH-054 stated that he was taken to Velepromet on the 21st of November and was searched by a soldier and reservist. He noted that three prisoners were taken away by paramilitaries and never returned. That's P02032, paragraphs 44-45. In the submissions on Monday, counsel referred to the evidence of GH-063, Mr. Karlovic. He was quoted -- Karlovic was quoted by the Defence at page 9016 of Monday's hearing, stating that "the JNA military police was in charge of guarding us," that statement being attributed to Karlovic. That's referring to page 8674 of Karlovic's trial testimony. However, the Defence failed to provide Your Honours with the remainder of Karlovic's evidence on that point. He said, and it's on the same page, 8674: "There is no procedure. The JNA military police was in charge of guarding us. However, the Chetniks had no problem entering the two rooms we were in and taking people out. Quite simply, the JNA military police, in co-operation with the Chetniks, had organised for those people to be taken out and killed." So it's our position, Mr. President, the evidence supports that both components, volunteers as well as JNA, were working together or certainly facilitating the activities of each other at Velepromet. Members of the Guards Brigade Motorised Brigade security organ, the Guards Motorised Brigade military police, and members of the Territorial Defence were present at Velepromet on the 19th of November; that is, P02284, paragraphs 51, 56; also transcript 6390. In front of the hangars where the detainees were held, there were two sets of guards, JNA military police, and Chetniks. This is P02284, paragraph 58-59. During a visit by the international diplomat and negotiator Herbert Okun, who was part of the delegation of Cyrus Vance, a visit to Vukovar on the 19th of November, 1991, more specifically at the reception centre there, it was noted that the centre was full of JNA and other rough customers, armed irregulars, and others. According to Okun there was an air of brooding and imminent menace conveyed by Chetnik-types. The JNA and irregular forces were intermingled and smoking cigarettes together. P1332.1325, page 33; P1325, transcript 16917 and 16919, that's Okun's 92 quater statement I'm referring to. GH-054 testified that a JNA captain came on the 21st of November, took him to the room of death. The captain said that they were all in danger of getting killed that night. This is 2032, paragraph 46. The room of death that the Chamber's heard a lot of evidence about P02056.1, transcript 5923-5924. Witness 54 gave evidence, I'm going to refer to at transcript 5498 and also P2038, regarding the identities of various victims who were in the room of death, among whom was Tihomir Perkovic, who was killed; that's at GH-063's evidence at trial transcript 8675. 8676, GH-063, Karlovic, tells his own story about when the Chetniks came into the room and took the 14-year-old boy, had him remove his clothes before taking him out and killing him. The JNA leadership in Vukovar, including Mrksic and Sljivancanin, were aware of the beatings and killings occurring at Velepromet on the night of the 19th of November, 1991. That's agreed fact or possibly adjudicated fact, I should say, adjudicated fact 157. Also P2284, paragraph 81-83. That night, Sljivancanin told members of the security administration: "Don't be surprised if Chetniks are slaughtering Ustashas there." That's 2284, paragraph 49-50; trial transcript 6353. So on the basis of all this, Mr. President, it's our position then that the JNA, being in charge of the Velepromet, the evidence indicating that JNA personnel were guarding prisoners and yet at the same time making the prisoners available to Chetniks for purposes of beatings and murders, these are linked through to JCE membership, the JCE membership on the one hand and the Chetnik volunteers through to Seselj's Serbian Radical Party on the other, committing crimes which are within the intended scope of the JCE of which Hadzic is a member. I'd like to just spend my last few minutes directing the Chamber's attention to some pieces of evidence which relate to Hadzic's authorities and his role, contribution, in respect of some of the other JCE actors whose crimes were taking place throughout the SBWS region. As we said in our legal submissions, it's not necessary to prove that Hadzic contributed in some direct way to each criminal incident. What is required is his proof of a significant contribution to the common criminal purpose. Hadzic used his powers and authorities as prime minister of the SBWS government and the support he received from the Serbian leadership in Belgrade to contribute to the common criminal purpose, which encompassed the crimes in this case including the specific incidents alleged challenged by counsel in their 98 bis submissions. As prime minister, according to GH-016, Hadzic possessed the powers typical exercised by prime ministers from around the world, but the powers were augmented due to the state of immediate threat of war in SBWS. That's transcript 1106-1108, and 1236. Witnesses universally testified that Hadzic was in command of the Serbian National Security unit, SNB, that was led by Stevo Bogic. For example, P1040, paragraphs 37-39 and 41; transcript 2825-2826; P140, paragraphs 94-95; P111, paragraphs 79 and 80; P246, which is a 92 ter statement, the transcript reference there 15201; and P201.140. Hadzic selected members of his SBWS government, that's GH-016, P140, paragraph 20. He proposed presidents of the municipal councils who were approved by his government, P197.140, including the -- Mr. -- the appointment of Mr. Borislav Zivanovic to be president of the Beli Manastir Executive Council. The Chamber may recall that it was Zivanovic and the Beli Manastir authorities which had passed a number of highly discriminatory pieces of legislation against non-Serbs residing in the Beli Manastir region during the latter part of 1991, referring here to P2157, 2158, 2160. The effects of the discriminatory legislation were described at transcript 5827-37. We know that Hadzic used his position and support to obtain needed equipment, manpower, and materials for the Serb forces that were conducting the crimes on the ground in the SBWS. Witness Djordjevic gave evidence of the trip that Hadzic and Arkan made to Belgrade in November of 1991, in which they met at the Serbian Ministry of Defence with Djordjevic who was acting on the co-ordination group of the Ministry of Defence. Hadzic requested 30- or 40.000 grenades. He was provided a smaller quantity of grenades for a different weapon. That's P2300, paragraph 71. Hadzic ordered that the Erdut training centre expenses be covered out of the funds of the DP Dalj agricultural enterprise, the place where Arkan was based. Pursuant to Hadzic's order, Arkan's training centre was financed by DP Dalj. P215.140 and P214.140. Hadzic had command over the SAO SBWS police and he exercised his authority to appoint and dismiss members of the police, P111, paragraphs 29-34; transcript 881, 884, 972 and 975. My colleague, Ms. Clanton, will address further issues regarding the SBWS police and Mr. Hadzic's relationship with it. As prime minister, Hadzic was Commander-in-Chief of the SBWS TO, T 1218, T 8283, 8292-93, 8378-8380; P1327, transcript of which is 17119-120; and P2913.1, paragraphs 98-99. That's the authority supporting that Hadzic was the Commander-in-Chief of the SBWS TO. Hadzic appointed Radovan Stojicic, Badza, as commander of the SBWS TO, P140, paragraph 48; transcript page 2645-2649. Witness Djordjevic of the Serbian Ministry of Defence gave evidence that as Croatia withdrew from the SFRY, presidents of the SAOs in Croatia filled the void that would have been otherwise filled by the president of the republic in respect of the TOs. He says at P2300, paragraph 8: "Presidents of the SAOs with their assemblies and structures became responsible under the law for organising and equipping the TOs in their territories." This means that for the SAO SBWS, it was Hadzic who was responsible for organising and equipping the SBWS Territorial Defence. We know that Badza, Stojicic, whom Hadzic appointed, was a high-level government of the MUP, Ministry of the Interior, of Serbia; and that once he arrived in the SBWS Stojicic attended meetings of Hadzic's SBWS government. P2913, paragraph 100; see also L38, page 3; and P197.140. One witness said that Hadzic and Stojicic regularly attended meetings together approximately every few days, P246, transcript 15186. GH-027 testified that Hadzic resisted taking on active-duty JNA officers as commanders of the SBWS TO. And as a result, no senior active-duty JNA officers were appointed as commanders of TO staffs in the SBWS. Instead, the SBWS TO officers were local taxi-drivers and labourers, and this was one of the ways in which Hadzic maintained control over what he referred to as "their" TO. That's P2913.1, paragraphs 98-99; transcript 8161-62; P2959.2913. That evidence is consistent with the evidence of GH-068 -- excuse me, GH-168, a witness who counsel spent quite a bit of time attempting to discredit in his submissions on Monday. On this point, GH-168's testimony is completely consistent with the testimony not only that I've just cited, but also to the testimony of Djordjevic of the Serbian Ministry of Defence. 168 testified that the SBWS leadership headed by Hadzic set up TO staffs to assist with the implementation of the plan to create Greater Serbia. He said that Hadzic's government selected staff members and subordinate units on that basis of the membership and loyalty to the SDS and their willingness to carry out any task. That's transcript 8282-8284; 8292-93; 8375, 8378-80. Djordjevic, who's co-ordination group was tasked to provide support to the TOs in Croatia, gave evidence that as opposed to the SAO Krajina, in 1991 the SBWS TO had limited dealings with the Serbian Ministry of Defence, again consistent with what's being said by 168 and also GH-027. Djordjevic said that he believed the SBWS TO dealt more closely with the JNA and possibly the Serbian MUP because Stojicic, Badza, was also himself a member of the Serbian MUP. P2300, paragraph 21. Brief few words on the volunteer unit Leva Supoderica and Arkan. P194.140, Hadzic, as SBWS prime minister, exercised his authority in appointing Arkan as commander of the Erdut training centre. P140, paragraphs 98, 100-101; also transcript 1218, 2650-2651. More generally, Witness GH-010 testified that volunteer units arriving in the SBWS placed themselves under the SBWS TO; that's transcript 4813-14; P1739; P1740. Exhibit 1727 indicates -- identifies Leva Supoderica as being one of these units comprised of volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party. They were dispatched from Belgrade. Its commander was Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni. This document, 1727 bears the stamp of the Vukovar TO staff. 2576, dated the 9th of November, 1991, to Kameni was commanding Leva Supoderica personnel as part of the Vukovar operation, receives this letter indicating additional volunteers are being dispatched to be placed "under the protection of the Vukovar TO." P151, on the 21st of January, 1992, Hadzic issued a decision disbanding the Leva Supoderica at the proposal of an assistant commander of the Novi Sad Corps. Hadzic issued the call welcoming volunteers from Serbia to come into the SBWS and to join the Serb forces already engaged there. He enthusiastically thanked them for their support and contribution, P58, transcript 610-612. My last remarks are about the Serbian National Security unit, the SNB, an elite unit that was formed for purposes of providing security to Hadzic. They were based in the Erdut training centre in the government offices. They were led by Stevo Bogic. P1040, paragraphs 54-61, 79; transcript 2895-2896. Bogic reported directly to Hadzic, 1040, paragraph 37, 38. There is a close connection between Bogic and the SNB, their personnel, and members of Arkan's Tigers, some of Arkan's Tigers received the SNB identification cards which enabled them to move throughout the area more freely even beyond the curfew time. P1040, paragraph 58. Members of the SNB acting jointly with some of Arkan's Tigers committed some of the most brutal and cold-blooded murders charged in this case. They also participated in brutal interrogations and torture, taking place with Arkan and Milorad Stricevic in the training centre. Members of Hadzic's SNB arrested and murdered Juliana Pap, Franjo Pap and Natalia Rakin, whose deaths are charged in paragraph 28 and whose bodies were dumped into the well outside Borovo Selo, that the Chamber visited a few months ago. Could I briefly go into closed session or private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, unless the Chamber has any questions, that completes my submissions at this point. I propose to give the floor to my colleague, Ms. Clanton, who will continue with our response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. President. As Mr. Stringer has explained, at the Rule 98 bis stage the question for Your Honours is whether the Prosecution has adduced enough evidence for each count taken as a whole, as opposed to an examination of all of the various charges making up the particular count. The Prosecution submits that it has presented evidence establishing each of the incidents charged in the indictment beyond a reasonable doubt. However, since it is unnecessary to establish the sufficiency of the evidence for every incident at this stage, our next submissions will focus on particular crimes and events that illustrate that the Prosecution's evidence is indeed capable of sustaining a conviction for every count of the indictment. I would like to begin with the detention and murders that took place in the Dalj police buildings. These crimes fall under Counts 1 through 9 of the indictment. The Chamber has heard evidence about the murders of at least 39 people in Dalj over the course of a two-week period in September and October of 1991. These crimes shocked the community and further intimidated the remaining non-Serb population of Dalj and the surrounding villages. As shocking as they were, these killings were not random or isolated incidents. The evidence shows that these crimes were part of the pattern of crimes committed against non-Serbs to force them from the territory and ensure that they would not return. Beginning with paragraph 24, the murder of 11 persons on September 21st, 1991. By the time of this crime, Dalj had already fallen into the hands of Serb forces and was serving as the seat of Hadzic's government. The forceful take-over of Dalj on the 1st of August, 1991, was part of what Hadzic described on the radio as the "decisive attack" on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, which had been planned in July of 1991. T 8291-8292; P2987; transcript page 1284-1285. In September 1991, non-Serb civilians who had been arrested in Baranja were transferred by the SBWS and Serbian police through Serbia to Borovo Selo. They joined other non-Serb civilians who had been arrested from Dalj, Erdut, Aljmas, and the respective hill areas or "planina" of each of those villages. All of the arrests were arbitrary, no criminal reports, detention orders, or other paperwork were provided for the detainees. As the Chamber heard, this transfer of non-Serb detainees from Banja and other parts of the SBWS to Dalj was done pursuant to Hadzic's orders. This included his own assertion when confronted about the status of these people that he was the prime minister and could order that anything be done. That's P111, paragraphs 49-54; transcript 5821-5822. Some prisoners from Baranja were then taken to Dalj, where they were first detained at the cultural centre and then to the local co-operative or Zadruga building that was serving as the Dalj police area. While in these Dalj police buildings, the detainees were frequently interrogated and savagely beaten almost every night. In particular, they were beaten and interrogated by Milorad Stricevic and his so-called space police, who were notorious for taking people away, interrogating them, physically mistreating them and liquidating them, P278, paragraphs 9-10; P111, paragraphs 47 and 65. A few days into their imprisonment, Arkan arrived at the facility and swore at the detainees, calling them Ustashas. He was together with Marko Loncarevic, a former policeman who co-ordinated the work of the TO staffs of the SBWS, as well as several men in camouflage uniform, Arkan's men. After introducing himself to the detainees, Arkan, that is, his men beat them severely with iron chairs until the chairs fell apart, P2132, page 7; P2110, page 5. During the night of the 21st to the 22nd of September, Hadzic and Arkan arrived at the police building along with approximately 20 of Arkan's men. After introducing himself to the detainees, Hadzic ordered that two of the men be released to him and left the remaining 11 prisoners to Arkan and his men, P250.245; P2132, pages 8-9. The Trial Chamber will recall that Hadzic had earlier attended a meeting with Arkan and journalist Aernout van Lynden in Belgrade, during which Arkan openly stated that he took no prisoners and told van Lynden that he would not be able to film if he killed prisoners. This is a statement that Arkan publicly repeated throughout the international media, transcript page 7029; P102. It therefore could not have come as a surprise to Hadzic or to anyone else that the 11 detainees were executed by Arkan and his men after they were removed from the Dalj police station. Hadzic's responsibility for this incident did not cease at the time that the non-Serbs whom he brought to Dalj were killed. He is further responsible for covering up this crime and preventing an investigation. Mr. President, if we could go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Approximately two weeks after the murder of 11 persons, at least 28 prisoners detained in the Dalj police station were killed by Milorad Stricevic, Arkan, and their men. This incident appears at paragraph 25 of the indictment. As with the previous 11 victims, many of the 28 victims had been brought from Baranja, P111, paragraph 62. There is evidence before this Chamber that during the first week of October 1991, Hadzic knew that the non-Serb prisoners were being held in the Dalj police buildings. Indeed, Hadzic and Arkan were seen talking in front of the detention facility in the days immediately before the killing of the prisoners, P278, paragraph 11. On the evening of the 4th of October, 1991, Arkan, Stricevic, and 20 of Arkan's men arrived at the station. For several hours in the early morning, the prisoners were beaten and then most were killed. A few prisoners were kept alive in order to load the bodies onto a truck which drove them to the river's edge. There the remaining prisoners were executed and all of the bodies were dumped in the river. Upon learning of this crime the next day, the Dalj police leadership conducted a preliminary inquiry and reported the incident of the SBWS police chain of command. This is P112.111; P111, paragraphs 65-72; P1140.1, page 4; P1141.1, transcript page 4166. These killings were known throughout Dalj within a day or so after they took place. Civilian medical staff were asked to retrieve four or five bodies that were stuck in the rocks as the water-level had dropped. Blood was visible on these rocks. Bodies were seen floating in the river, P104; P253, paragraph 82. The townspeople of Dalj kept reporting this information to the police. Around the 10th of October, 1991, Arkan made a speech in the Dalj market square in front of hundreds of persons, including representatives of the JNA, the SBWS government, and SBWS TO and police officials, acknowledging that he had killed the prisoners and stating that no one could do anything to him. He announced that his philosophy was "a tooth for a tooth and an eye for an eye." This was widely known in the community. T 1543, 1546-1549; P111, paragraphs 68, 75-76. This all occurred while Hadzic maintained his government offices less than a kilometre from the crime scene and a couple hundred metres from the Dalj market square, transcript page 769-787. Despite the uproar in Dalj and the actions taken by the police in this instance, no actions were taken to punish the perpetrators. The same Serb forces who murdered the detainees in late September and early October participated in forcing the remaining non-Serbs of Dalj from their homes and they plundered their property. This pertains to Counts 10 through 14 of the indictment. I have just one example. In October 1991, the same month as the killing of the 28 prisoners, remaining Croats in Dalj were gathered in busses and expelled. GH-169 explained that the expulsions of the Croats from Dalj were organised and were similar to the expulsions that took place in other towns such as Vukovar, transcript 8793-8797. He also testified that this happened again and again. Buildings of religious significance to the Croat community, such as the Catholic church in Dalj, were mined and destroyed by Arkan's men, transcript 8735-8736. The mistreatment I've described, that is, the mistreatment of the non-Serb civilian inhabitants of Dalj and surrounding areas, is consistent with the widespread expulsions, deportation, imprisonments, torture, wanton destruction, plunder, and persecution inflicted on the non-Serb residents of many towns in the SBWS and throughout what would later become the RSK in 1991 and 1993. This mistreatment featured prominently as well in the nearby town of Erdut where Arkan established his training centre. Mr. Stringer has already spoken today about the contributions of the accused to the JCE, including his role in assigning the Erdut training centre to Arkan, who became its commander. Now I will briefly speak about the violent crimes and the environment of fear that characterised Arkan and his training centre and the concordance between the functions of the training centre and the counts in the indictment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down for the purposes of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I apologise. The Concordance between the functions of the training centre and the counts in the indictment, including but not limited to Counts 3-9. The Erdut training centre was the epicentre of the activities of Arkan and his men. They lived there, they ate there, and they trained there. The facility was also next to that used by Hadzic, for the government and for Hadzic's personal security service, the SNB. When not travelling to Serbia, Hadzic would spend the night at the training centre, transcript page 2705-2706. The installation by Hadzic of Arkan and his men at the training centre served several purposes. First and foremost, this facility was used to further the campaign of removing non-Serbs from Slavonia and surrounding areas. The men who were trained at the centre, like Arkan himself, were known criminal and they lived up to their reputation. I refer the Chamber to P2916. At the training centre, they imprisoned, mistreated, tortured, and murdered non-Serbs. The non-Serbs were detained in poor conditions, including what had been the public restrooms. Their space by 4 by 4 metres, and was damp, dark, and cold. They were provided no bedding and were unable to sleep. They were repeatedly taken to Milorad Stricevic for interrogation and many came back badly beaten. They were removed in the middle of the night from their cell, lined up against a wall, and then subjected to a mock execution. During the nights, members of Arkan's men took prisoners from the room. Shortly thereafter, the prisoners remaining heard gun-shots and the people who were taken were never seen again. This continued until a room holding 28 men contained only two. Transcript page 2686, 2701-2703; 2207-2214, 2227. Arkan's men targeted the remaining Croat male population of Erdut and surrounding villages. Many of these men had been forced to labour, that is, as forced labourers in the months before they were taken from their homes and ultimately brought to the training centre and killed. But they did not target only men. The Chamber has heard evidence that non-Serb women were also detained and mistreated at the centre. The prisoners included a woman of 65 years who was kept in a robe and slippers, P2039; transcript 2702. Arkan's men, working with Milorad Stricevic and Erdut local police, including Bozo Bolic, decimated the ethnic Hungarian population of the Planina region of Dalj, Erdut, and Aljmas. All the men of several families were taken and killed. The wives of the victims were told by Bolic that their husbands and their fathers were in Arkan's hands and that they should not try to go see them. Ominously, they were told that their husbands and fathers would not be requiring medication or warm coats anymore. The training centre employees testified that the Hungarians were kept in detention at the training centre where they were forced to sing the Serb national anthem. The Hungarians were taken away. Transcript 2174-2176, 2193, 2701. By November 1991, it was public knowledge in the eastern Slavonia region that prisoners taken to the Erdut training centre never returned, transcript page 2208. The Erdut training centre served to support the widespread commission of crimes against civilians with the purpose of creating a state without non-Serbs. It is important to emphasise that the training centre itself and the forces located there facilitated the removal of the non-Serb population in another way: Through sheer intimidation. Even those who were not detained at the centre feared for their lives and knew that anyone could be taken at any time. The behaviour and reputation of Arkan's men was such that their daily activities spread fear. The Chamber has seen video of his men singing songs with lyrics such as: We will crush the Ustasha, we will kill them all. The Chamber has heard evidence that Arkan was relied on by other JCE members to operate in the field, engaging in retribution and intimidation, which was designed to rid the area of non-Serbs, P129; P331, paragraphs 11-12; transcript page 8282-8283, and 8295-8297. Your Honours, the crimes I've just described that were committed in Dalj and Erdut, part of eastern Slavonia, they did not take place in isolation. The crimes in Slavonia in 1991 were part of the plan that was executed in the entire territory of the SBWS. The Prosecution has shown that the crimes that were committed and charged in the indictment all took place in the context of the execution of the common criminal plan to expel non-Serbs. As we have stated several times, consideration of individual incidents is inappropriate for Rule 98 bis. However, the sake of assisting Your Honours, I will now discuss the mistakes in counsel's submissions about -- submissions on Monday concerning the testimony of GH-012; then I will discuss the evidence showing the single JCE and the links between bodies in Western Srem and the government; finally, I'll turn to the remaining crime bases identified by Defence counsel, Opatovac and Lovas. On Monday, counsel suggested, page 8971, that the accused is not responsible for certain crimes committed in the area of what was described as OG South. In particular, counsel suggested that the testimony of GH-012, Dusan Jaksic, proves that there were no links between the SBWS government and the TO units and TO staffs located in Vukovar and in Western Srem. Jaksic's testimony does not support this claim. Further, the recitation of his evidence of counsel was selective and ignores the totality of the evidence of the relationship between the accused and events that occurred south of the Vuka river. Counsel's interpretation of Jaksic's evidence is highly strained. Counsel conflated the concepts of TO units and TO staffs. While TO units could and were resubordinated to OG South and Colonel Mrksic during combat, the TO staffs themselves were not. Transcript page 7063-7064, 7109-7110. This is part of Jaksic's testimony and I refer the Chamber to that in particular related to his description of the political functions and the position of commanders of the TO staff. In this context, Your Honours, Jaksic's testimony that the TO staffs were civilian political institutions that reported to the Ministry of Defence is entirely consistent with his evidence that the Petrova Gora TO unit was resubordinated to OG South. In fact, Jaksic testified that he was appointed TO Staff Commander for the OG South area, not by the JNA, but rather at a meeting of village TO staff commanders held in Oriolik. Transcript page 7063-7064, 7109. Other witness evidence presented in this trial also supports that the various local TO staffs within the SAO SBWS remained under civilian control, even when their TO units were temporarily resubordinated to the JNA for combat operations. Transcript page 8283-8293; P140, paragraphs 40-41. The Chamber has also received into evidence documents that establish that the TO staffs in Vukovar and Western Srem were operating under the SBWS government, in co-operation with the JNA. The following are exhibits that show these links: P1727, is dated 18th of October, 1991, a document of the SBWS TO, issued by Dusan Filipovic in Sid that legalised the Leva Supoderica detachment as part of the Vukovar TO. D6, D6 is the minutes of a 30th of October, 1991, meeting in Lovas that was attended by TO staff and village representatives of, among other villages, Lovas, Opatovac, Sotin, and Tovarnik. The minutes show that the meeting was also attended by several members of the SBWS government, including Mladen Hadzic, Ilija Petrovic, Stevo Bogic, Borislav Bogunovic, and Vojin Susa. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, is listed as attending as the SBWS TO commander. Mladen Hadzic chaired this meeting and during the meeting he explained how the SBWS government "is constantly working in this field" and that they had launched many "drives, actions, and tasks." Stevo Bogic insisted that it was the duty of the village representatives to inform the government of events. Ljuban Devetak of Lovas asked the SBWS government to recommend "the organisation of power in local communes ... the government must issue decrees about how we should get organised." The minutes of this meeting show the ability of the government to operate in the Western Srem area prior to the fall of Vukovar. P2979, this exhibit is the minutes of a 3rd of November, 1991, meeting also held in Lovas attended by TO staff and village representatives of the towns or villages of Opatovac, Mahovo, Lovas, Tovarnik, Sotin, and Vukovar. On this occasion, the meeting was led by Slobodan Grahovac, who was listed in the minutes as the deputy minister of the Serbian district of the SBWS. It was attended as well by Dusan Filipovic, a member of the SBWS TO staff. This evidence about the positions that were held by Grahovac and Filipovic is consistent with the testimony of witnesses before this Chamber, including Goran Stoparic, who stated that Grahovac was linked to the government and was described as a minister and the testimony of Borivoje Savic who said that Filipovic was the commander of the TO staff. I would refer the Chamber to P50, paragraph 205, and transcript page 4714, 4773-4774. The agenda of the meeting was the current problems of the Territorial Defence staffs in the liberated places. At the end of the meeting, the participants unanimously arrived at the following conclusions, and there are three that I want to share: First, to establish units and TO staffs in the liberated places "in accordance with the instructions and tables which the competent organs of the government worked out and sent out." Second, based on the organisation worked out per the previous item, to step up co-operation and co-ordination with the JNA. And third, that "existing and obvious problems have to be continuously resolved in co-operation with the government of this district and the relevant military command, such as the mop-up of the village and surrounding areas, freedom of movement, et cetera." General Vasiljevic testified about these minutes. He stated that the use of the term "co-operation" between the TO staffs and the JNA shows that: " These are activities of two sides that have an approximately equal status. So this is not a relationship between a subordinate and a superior. So that is co-operation in something that is in their common interest, two structures that co-ordinate their activities." Transcript page 8179-8184. For all of the reasons noted above, Your Honours, there is ample evidence in the record showing the links between Hadzic, his government, and the TO forces in the areas referred to on Monday as OG South. And I'm mindful of the time, perhaps we should ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Clanton. Court adjourned. We will be back at 12.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I am now going to discuss why the Defence arguments concerning Opatovac and Lovas also must fail. These towns are in Western Srem and Your Honours have heard evidence that they were taken by Serb forces in October 1991. For the village of Opatovac, the Defence has challenged the charges of imprisonment, torture, inhumane acts, and cruel treatment in Counts 5 through 9. For Lovas, the Defence has also challenged the charges of murder and extermination, Counts 1 through 4. For the village of Opatovac, the Defence pointed to the testimony of two witnesses at transcript page 9021 and 9022 of Monday's transcript. Based on the submissions of counsel, the Prosecution understood that the accused is not challenging the crimes themselves, but rather his responsibility for them. I should add that for now I am intentionally setting aside the quotation used from expert Reynaud Theunens that was provided to Your Honours on the submissions of Lovas and Opatovac. I will return to that issue when we speak about Lovas. With regard to Opatovac at page 9021, counsel listed certain of the evidence about who the perpetrators were and what they did. Then he suggested that there is no evidence that the accused intended these crimes or that the crimes were encompassed through a joint criminal enterprise of which he was a member. This is at page 9022. My colleague, Mr. Stringer, has already discussed the existence of the JCE in which the accused was a member. He has also clarified for Your Honours the correct legal framework, including that the accused need not be aware of all the details of the specific criminal incidents as a JCE member in order to be found responsible. Now, turning to the facts that were presented by counsel, the witness evidence concerning some of the perpetrators in Opatovac is indeed Prosecution evidence of the commission of crimes by members of the JCE and the forces that utilised them. The evidence you heard on Monday shows that units of the JNA and the local Territorial Defence, aided by local Serbs, participated in the crimes in Opatovac. In addition, the Chamber heard evidence during this trial that soldiers from Kragujevac were present in Opatovac, as were paramilitary or Chetnik groups who threatened the population. Transcript page 8626 and 8642. The evidence before Your Honours of the crimes committed in Opatovac mirrors the broader pattern of crimes in Western Srem. I would like to briefly remind you of the evidence that you have heard about the pattern of crimes committed by JCE members or persons utilised by them in Western Srem. For this I will mention the evidence of four witnesses as an illustration. First, the former commander of the police force in Ilok testified that the pattern was as follows: First, the JNA issued tough ultimatums; then it indiscriminately shelled; then its forces entered the towns, followed by reservists and local Serbs. This method caused the inhabitants of the town to flee. When the reservists and local Serbs entered towns, they would abuse villagers physically and psychologically and they would kill some of them. That's at page 3487-3488, P1418 at transcript page 1313. Next, the Chamber also heard evidence that the crimes did not stop at killings and physical and psychological abuse. Witness Tomislav Rukavina, a resident of Bapska, verified that the non-Serbs remaining in Western Srem in early 1992 were then forced to leave. When they left, they confirmed what had happened in their village. After the Serb army subdued the village, the village was left to paramilitaries. These paramilitaries would break into their homes, threaten their lives, force them to sign documents which stated that they were willingly moving to Croatia, strip them of their personal possessions and valuables, and then force them to leave. Transcript page 2130; P327 and P328. Third, Your Honours heard the evidence of James Lubin, a civilian affairs co-ordinator for UNPROFOR in Sector East. He testified that prior to his arrival non-Serbs were mistreated in the manner I've just described consistent with P328. He added to that that the description is incomplete because in some cases the expulsions were happening on a daily and even hourly basis. Mr. Lubin testified that some people were physically beaten and were in a very bad state when they were expelled. He said that they were crying and shaking with fear, obviously terrified for their lives. Transcript page 3196. Finally, Your Honours heard evidence that some non-Serbs from Opatovac and other villages were unable to reach safety when they were expelled from their villages. They were sent to the Sid military prison, to Begejci camp, to Stajicevo farm and the Zrenjanin barracks, P2993, page 6; P2992, page 9. Dr. Mladen Loncar testified that the older women, those who were not of child-bearing age, in the Begejci detention camp were from the towns of Western Srem, including Tovarnik, Ilok, Lovas, Berak, Sarengrad, and Bapska. This is at transcript page 8231. Your Honours, these witnesses, Mr. Rukavina, Mr. Brletic, and Mr. Lubin, all confirmed that persons from Opatovac, non-Serb persons from Opatovac were victimised in this way. This is at transcript page 2130, 3488, and 3196 respectively. The underlying criminal incidents in Opatovac fall squarely within the JCE. Next, Your Honours, I would like to move on to Lovas and address the shortcomings of the Rule 98 bis challenge to the crimes that were committed in Lovas. The argument made by counsel about the Lovas minefield crime which is paragraph 26 of the indictment contains errors that are similar to those in his submissions on Opatovac. In addition, the Defence has challenged the relationship between named members of the Serb authorities in Lovas, such as Ljuban Devetak and the government. The Defence has also challenged whether the accused could be liable for crimes that took place when he was not physically present at the scene of the crime. This is transcript page 9010-9013 of Monday's hearing. As Mr. Stringer has already discussed the errors in legal submissions and has emphasised for Your Honours that there is no requirement for the accused to have knowledge of every incident, that is, every murder that takes place, I will focus my submissions on some of the key evidence which shows the responsibility of the accused for crimes committed in Lovas, also including evidence before Your Honours about the relationship between the authorities in Lovas and JCE members. This forms part of Counts 2 through 9. Inhabitants of Lovas were not the only persons who were present during the attack that began on the 10th of October. Some of the people in Lovas on that day had come to Lovas after fleeing neighbouring towns that had already been attacked, such as Tovarnik, Ilaca, and Berak, transcript page 1653 to 1654. The pattern of crimes that I have just discussed and the submissions on Opatovac feature prominently in the attack on Lovas. Your Honours have heard evidence of negotiations that did not succeed, an ultimatum, then shelling, including of religious buildings, followed by an attack, including killings, before the ultimate take-over of the town. The take-over occasioned forced labour, unlawful detention, and additional crimes such as the murder and torture of non-Serbs. Witness Zeljko Cirba testified that after the village was taken over, all villagers of Croatian nationality and non-Serbs had to report for interrogations and they were sometimes detained for days at a time. Croats and non-Serbs were obliged to wear a white ribbon on their sleeve marking their ethnic origin and constantly taken for interrogation and mistreatment. They were also subject to the work detail. This is at P288, paragraph 27. The killing in the minefield was perpetrated by members of the Valjevo TO detachment from Serbia and the Dusan Silni. The Dusan Silni, a unit led by Devetak, was active in the Western Srem area and consisted of men from the Stara Pazova area who supported Mirko Jovic's Serbian National Renewal Party. They operated in Lovas alongside the TO and the JNA and with the civilian authorities led by Devetak. This is P2913.1, paragraph 80; transcript page 7951; transcript page 1822-1824; P1865. The evidence shows that Serb civilian authorities took over Lovas very soon after the attack. Various witnesses have given evidence about these authorities in Lovas. Witness Ivan Mujic described these people, these authorities, in plain language. He said Devetak was the number one person in the village and that Milan Radojcic was his right-hand man. Transcript page 1703-1704. Radojcic was the commander of the Lovas TO, P2979, P300, paragraph 46. General Vasiljevic confirmed that the JNA had no part in the appointment of Ljuban Devetak, transcript page 8180. P2979, which I've already referred to, again this exhibit is the minutes of the meeting on the 3rd of November in Lovas. The attendees were the local civilian leaders, TO commanders, Dusan Filipovic of the SBWS TO staff, and representatives of the government, police, and JNA. During this meeting - this is on page 6 of the English and 6 of the B/C/S of P2979 - Devetak listed the problems in Lovas and stated that: "Our government should urgently get in touch with the JNA and solve all these problems." Now, the positions held by Ljuban Devetak and Milan Radojcic are further explained in a JNA report to the 1st Military District which is dated the 28th of February, 1992. This is Exhibit D51. In this document, on page 4 of the English and of the B/C/S, the JNA reports that Serb refugees from Western Slavonia are moving into the municipalities of Mirkovci and Vukovar. Colonel Novica Gusic, the assistant commander for civilian affairs, stated the following and this is a quote: "Because of distrust and what is happening to the Serbs who remained in Western Slavonia and their property, and with the tacit consent of the government of the SAO Slavonia and the assistance of the prominent members of the government, the so-called co-ordinators and ministers, they are placing a certain pressure on the local inhabitants to make them move out voluntarily. In doing so, they resorted to unlawful means, threats, and even killed some individuals. Characteristic examples of such conduct can be found in the villages of Bapska, Lovas, Sarengrad, and Mahovo, organised by Radojcic from Lovas village, the commander of the Lovas Territorial Defence Staff and co-ordinator for the TO 5th Zone who has behind him a certain Ljuban Devetak, who is very influential in the government of the SAO Slavonia." Your Honours, these excerpts of documents are meant to provide examples of the links between the government, other members of the JCE, and the crimes that were committed in Lovas. This is not an exhaustive list. Witness and documentary evidence show that the crimes in Lovas, including the murders in the minefield, were part of the plan to remove non-Serbs. After the minefield incident, those who survived who were able to leave, had to sign a document turning over their property to the government, that's at transcript page 1822-1826 and 1828. Some of those persons who were put through the minefield were expelled in December of 1991, P1083, paragraphs 58 and 59. Witness Ivan Mujic testified that at least one person who was wounded in the minefield was tortured in a cellar in Lovas in December of 1991 before being forcibly expelled, this is P296, transcript page 1706-1707, and P292.287. Your Honours, turning now to the argument put forth by counsel for Opatovac and Lovas concerning the role of town commands and the testimony of expert Reynaud Theunens. This is at transcript page 9011 and 9022 from Monday's hearing. Mr. Theunens' evidence on town commands, as well as that of town commander Colonel Milorad Vojnovic and General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, makes clear that the JNA was not in charge of civilian affairs in the areas mentioned by counsel. Instead, the civil affairs organs of the JNA were co-operating with the civilian authorities in the area, that is, the government and its representatives. I would refer Your Honours to P2943; transcript pages T 5106-5109; P1981, paragraphs 24 and 25; transcript pages 7956 to 7961 and 8169-8170. During this hearing, the Prosecution will not address every single factual misrepresentation or inaccuracy from the presentation we heard on Monday. One in particular, however, relates to the mis-characterisation of Mr. Theunens' evidence. Counsel parsed a 20-plus-page exchange that took place during Mr. Theunens' testimony and claimed that Mr. Theunens testified that the civilian authorities did not have authority over civilian affairs. This discussion starts on transcript page 4572. In fact, Mr. Theunens testified that there were consultations and co-ordination between the town command and the SAO SBWS authorities. This is at transcript page 4575.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Further, Your Honours, using the specific examples that were put forward by counsel during his cross-examination of Mr. Theunens, Mr. Theunens stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I hope that this one will be the last one, Ms. Clanton. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I should go back a sentence. What I was saying, Your Honours, is that during his cross-examination Mr. Theunens, using the specific examples that Defence counsel put to Mr. Theunens, Theunens stated that the documents indicate that the civilian authorities, that is, the government, had responsibility for most civilian matters. And this is at transcript page 4583-4585. And, Your Honours, this concludes our response to the submissions made by counsel on Monday. For all of the reasons put forward by the Prosecution today, the Chamber should deny the Rule 98 bis motion seeking a judgement of acquittal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Clanton. This is the end of the Rule 98 bis hearings. Court is adjourned until further notice.
